s03.slug: TUESDAY · 1:15 PM · THE SOCCER STADIUM OVERFLOW LOT, CSU MARISOL
s03.music: The Ting Tings — “Shut Up and Let Me Go”
body: January sun comes flat across the overflow lot behind the soccer stadium: eleven acres of white lines painted for game days, light poles throwing short shadows at a quarter past one, and in the middle of it the Saab with its top down, the only car on the asphalt. Her iPod is plugged into the tape deck through the adapter, the cord looped once around the gearshift, and the Ting Tings are coming out of the door speakers louder than a car this old was built to take.

She has wanted to teach him stick since December. The Saab is a manual, and everything Jack has ever driven — his father’s Silverado, the driver’s-ed Taurus at Mooney with a second brake on the passenger side — has shifted for him. Skye is sideways in the passenger seat in his flannel over a tank top, sunglasses pushed up into her hair, feet up on the dash with her toes against the windshield, giving instruction.

“Clutch is the one on the left. You let it out like you’re giving somebody bad news,” she says. “Slow, slow, and then all at once, and then you don’t apologize.” She holds up a finger. “House rule. Every time you stall, you owe me a voice. My choice.”
“What kind of voice?”
“Whoever I say. I’ll know if you phone it in.”
He stalls in eleven feet. The Saab bucks once, as if it’s been insulted, and dies, and the Ting Tings carry on without it.

“A Teamster taught me,” she says, “on the Warner lot, in a grip truck, when I was fourteen. I stalled it twenty times and he never said one word. He just ate his sandwich.” She turns the music down a hair. “I am not that man.”
“Your father,” Skye says.
He has only the one word of his father’s that she’d know, so he gives it everything: the chin down, the eyes on a television in Ohio, the voice up out of the bottom of a lunch pail. “Pryor.”
“Your father does it with his chin,” Skye says. “You did it with your eyebrows. Two.”
The second stall is Hale, from the description. “Costigan,” Jack says, all cut glass, “you have buggered the clutch, and I confess myself unsurprised.”
“That’s a pirate. Hale isn’t a pirate. Three, for *buggered*.”

For the third she wants the Pope blessing the Saab, and he says he isn’t doing a blessing for a bit, and she puts both hands up — “Fine, fine, he doesn’t bless it, he just *notices* it” — so he gives her Benedict XVI, gentle and Bavarian, confronted with a dented convertible in a parking lot: “It is… a very small car.”
She has to put her face in her hands. “He sounds so *sorry* for it. Four. I’d watch that Pope.”

body.text: Before he turns the key again she reaches across and touches him under the St. Michael, the place she knows now, and goes back to her own side of the car.

body: Four is Nonna, and he doesn’t have to think about it. “*Piano, piano*,” he says, with one hand going in a small circle over the wheel, the way hers goes over a pot.
“What’s it mean?”
“Slowly. Slowly.”
“Then why didn’t you?” She gives him a six. Nonna is his best, she tells him, and he is not allowed to get cocky about a woman who is eighty-four.
Five is Corinne. He narrows his eyes and works an invisible BlackBerry with his thumb: “Is that *employable*?”

“Wait.” Skye takes her phone off the dash. “You should hear the original.” She finds a voicemail from nine this morning and puts it on speaker, and holds it out between them over the gearshift, and Beverly Hills comes into the overflow lot, clipped and low.
“Skye. Corinne. About Sunday. That was a sighting we didn’t manage, and I’m not upset — I want to be very clear that I’m not upset. We’re going to let it breathe. Nothing new goes up. Call me.”

Skye deletes it with her thumb. “One. She’d fire you.” She lays the phone face-down on her knee and takes her feet off the dash. “She wants to let it breathe,” she says. “I’m going to let it breathe in front of everybody.”

After that the stalls come faster. Six is Ted — “Costigan, I owe you a kidney” — and she gives it a seven: “You’ve studied.” Seven is Gina, and he tries to do lowercase with his mouth and can’t, and Skye says Gina could. Eight is Doug Pruitt, *dude* stretched over five vowels until it comes apart, and she gives it a nine and makes him do it again just to hear it. Nine is her mother.
“Jack. *Jack.* Sit, sit, sit.”
Skye pulls her sunglasses down over her eyes. “Ten,” she says, from behind them. “Never again. I mean it.”

By then his left foot has found it: the place in the pedal’s travel where the clutch takes hold, a small shiver up through the sole of his shoe that means the car is listening. He gets her rolling in first along the painted lines, past one light pole and the next, and the engine climbs, and he pushes in and pulls the stick down and back and lets out, and the Saab goes into second like it was waiting to be asked. It doesn’t buck. It goes. Skye screams like he’s won a car on a game show.

body.text: He’s in second while she’s still taking the breath to say *now*. She points at him across the car. “You beat me to it. Again.”

body: She makes him bring it to a stop at the far fence — badly, but a stop — and comes across the console with the sunglasses knocked crooked and kisses him, one kiss, hers, with both fists in the front of his shirt, and sits back. “That’s the prize,” she says. “There’s only the one. Don’t get used to it.”
The song has gone around to the start again. She looks at him from her side of the car with her knees up.
“I’d like you to stall again.”
“I just learned not to.”
“I know.” She doesn’t blink. “I’d like to see what you look like when you do it on purpose.”
So he lets the clutch out too fast, on purpose, with his eyes on her, and the Saab shudders and quits against the fence.
“That one doesn’t count,” Skye says. “That one’s a gift.”

body.text: She doesn’t ask him for anything for it. She reaches over and puts her hand on his on the knob and leaves it there, and with the other hand she gets out the white iPhone.
body.else: “Do Ted again. Ted’s your best.” And while he’s doing Ted she gets out the white iPhone.

body: She holds it out at arm’s length across the console with its back to him, the one eye on his side of the car, where she can’t see the screen and doesn’t try. The shutter makes its fake little sound. Again. On the third he’s laughing — at her, at the phone, at the idea of himself in a picture — and she brings it in and looks. “That one.”
It’s him in her driver’s seat in the January light, laughing at something out of the frame, his hand still on the knob. He can’t remember what he was laughing at. It was her.
She types with her thumb, the tip of her tongue in the corner of her mouth, and doesn’t ask him, and turns the phone around when it’s done.

body: “Corinne said nothing new goes up,” Jack says.
“Corinne said a lot of things.” She drops the phone in the cup holder, face up, and swings her feet over the console into his lap, and the subject is closed.

She has other news anyway, off her phone, and tells it like gossip about a cousin. Conan O’Brien put out a statement today; she read it before she picked him up. NBC wants Leno back at 11:35 and *The Tonight Show* pushed to five minutes after midnight, and Conan won’t do it. He says he won’t be the one to move it out of the hour it’s had since before either of them was born, because it would hurt the show.
“It’s very well written,” Skye says. “Somebody good was up all night.”
“Good for him,” Jack says. “They promised him that show.”
“Did they?”

“Two thousand four. Leno said it on his own show: in five years, it’s Conan’s. On the air, in front of everybody.” He is Frank Costigan’s son; he believes in a man’s word the way he believes in the Browns, against experience. “That’s a promise. A promise is a promise.”

“NBC never promised Conan anything.” She counts it off with her toes against his thigh. “A network promised a time slot. Time slots aren’t people. In my business nobody can promise anybody anything — that’s what contracts are for. A contract is what everybody signs once everybody in the room has agreed not to mean it.”
“That’s bleak, Skye.”

“Ask Letterman. Carson retires, and everybody in Burbank thinks Letterman was promised that chair, and Letterman thinks so too, and Leno gets it because Leno was standing closest to the door.” She shrugs with her feet. “So Letterman goes to CBS and gets a lot of money in writing. That’s the happy ending. That’s the only kind we have.”
“Then Letterman should’ve got it in writing the first time.”
“*Thank* you.”
“It’s *healthy*. Everybody knows where they stand. At 12:05 nobody cries.” She tips her head back against the door frame and looks at him upside down. “And that’s what’s funny about Sunday.”
“Then Sunday wasn’t a promise either.”
She brings her head up and looks at him the right way round.
“Sunday wasn’t to a network.”

choices.text: “Then nobody in Burbank has ever meant anything.”
response: “Then nobody in Burbank has ever meant anything.”

“Correct.” She pulls the sunglasses off to look at him properly, delighted to be pushed. “Welcome to my hometown. We have a parade. It’s mostly lawyers.” She pokes him in the ribs with her big toe. “Now get us out of this lot without killing it.”

choices.text: “You’re right. A time slot can’t keep a promise.”
response: “You’re right. A time slot can’t keep a promise.”

“Only people can.” She sits up and holds out her phone. “Say it again. I want it in writing.” So he types it into her notes with one finger, hunting for every letter on the glass, and she reads it back to him in Corinne, and saves it.

choices.text: “Leno’s chin is the only thing in Burbank anybody can count on.”
response: “Leno’s chin is the only thing in Burbank anybody can count on.”

She laughs so hard her heel catches the middle of the wheel and the horn goes off, one long bleat across eleven acres of nothing. “Horn’s a stall,” she says when she can. “House rule. I owe you.” So she does him — the shoulders up, the Youngstown in the vowels, the chin — and gives him two words of it, flat as Ohio: “I’m good.”

s03a.slug: TUESDAY · 2:31 PM · OCEAN ROAD, THE SAAB, PULLED OVER BY THE GROVE
body: At twenty past two she put him back behind the wheel for what she called the real exam, Ocean Road to the Grove and back without dropping out of second, and at the first stop sign her iPod died in the middle of a song, and the adapter slid out of the deck, and the Saab’s own radio came up by itself on KCLU in the dead air between programs.

Now he has it in second along the bluff with the Pacific on his left, doing twenty-five like a man carrying a cake, and the radio is somebody promising a gardening show at three, and Skye has one arm out of the car riding the wind up and down.

At 2:31 by the clock in the dash the program stops and the news comes in over it. A powerful earthquake has struck near Port-au-Prince, Haiti, this afternoon. The Geological Survey puts it at magnitude seven. There is no word yet on casualties. Telephone lines into the country are down. The man reading it says that part twice.

He pulls over. He does it badly, onto the dirt turnout under the first of the eucalyptus at the edge of the Grove, with his foot on the brake and nothing on the clutch, and the Saab jerks and stalls. Skye reaches across and turns the key the rest of the way off.

It’s quiet without the engine. Long strips of bark let go of the trees overhead and come down on the hood and the windshield. On the radio a man in Washington says he has been trying to reach people in Port-au-Prince since the shaking and can’t get through to anyone: not his office, not his family. There have been aftershocks already, the radio says, strong ones, minutes apart. It’s a city of a couple of million people. It is half past five there, and it will be dark soon.
Skye has brought her arm back into the car. She turns the volume down a notch, and then turns it back up to where it was.
“Where is Haiti,” she says. “Exactly.”
She doesn’t dress it up. She doesn’t know, and she says so, and waits.

“Under Cuba. Down and to the right.” He draws it on the dash with his finger, a shape like a claw reaching west. “It’s half an island. The other half’s the Dominican Republic. Port-au-Prince is on this side, in the bay.”
“How do you know that?”

“Rice Bowl.” Every Lent at St. Brigid’s they sent you home with a cardboard box you folded up yourself, Catholic Relief Services printed across the top, and you put your quarters in it instead of buying candy, and Ma handed them out at the office window on Ash Wednesday and took them back at Easter, heavy, rattling. There was a map on the side. Some years the map was Haiti. “Poorest country in our half of the world. They make you find it before you can do long division.”
Skye looks out through the windshield, past the bark on the glass, at the ocean, as though Haiti were somewhere out there and she might see it if she looked long enough.
“Two million,” Skye says, to herself, as though she is checking she heard it.
A truck goes by on Ocean Road and the Saab rocks a little on its springs. On the radio the man reads it again from the top.

choices.text: *Cross yourself. Say the prayer out loud.*
choices.key: In the Saab, when the radio said Haiti, you crossed yourself and said a Hail Mary aloud. She asked for every word.
response: He crosses himself, forehead and heart and shoulders, there in the driver’s seat with his hands coming back to the wheel after, and says a Hail Mary, low, not hurrying it. Skye doesn’t look at the radio. She watches his mouth till he gets to the end.
“What was that?” she says. “The whole thing.”
He tells her, slowly, and she says the first half back to him: *Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you.* He gave it to her with *thee*. He doesn’t correct it.

At a quarter past three she takes the wheel back and drives him to his three-thirty with both hands on it, under the speed limit. At the curb on the Commons road she leans across and kisses him goodbye, short. “Text me when you’re out.” Her hand stays on his sleeve after the kiss, his cuff in her fingers, and then she lets go of it.

choices.text: *Take her hand. Turn the radio up.*
choices.key: In the Saab, when the radio said Haiti, you took her hand and turned the radio up.
response: He takes her hand off her knee and turns it palm up in his, and reaches over with the other and turns the radio up. They listen to the bulletin through to the end, and to the man in Washington again, and her thumb goes back and forth over his knuckles and doesn’t stop.

At a quarter past three she takes the wheel back and drives him to his three-thirty with both hands on it, under the speed limit. At the curb on the Commons road she leans across and kisses him goodbye, short. “Text me when you’re out.” Her hand stays on his sleeve after the kiss, his cuff in her fingers, and then she lets go of it.

choices.text: “My nonna’s already got her rosary out. I’d bet the car.”
choices.key: In the Saab, when the radio said Haiti, you told her your grandmother already had her rosary out.
response: “My nonna’s already got her rosary out,” he says. “I’d bet the car.”
“You don’t have a car.”
“Then your car.”
She laughs, small, through her nose. After that she’s quiet, and they listen.

At a quarter past three she takes the wheel back and drives him to his three-thirty with both hands on it, under the speed limit. At the curb on the Commons road she leans across and kisses him goodbye, short. “Text me when you’re out.” Her hand stays on his sleeve after the kiss, his cuff in her fingers, and then she lets go of it.

body: Theo is still out. His bed is made the way he made it at seven, the blazer gone off the back of his chair, and 412 is dark except for the little screen of the RAZR when it lights. Jack came up the east stairs at ten to twelve and lay down in his clothes on top of the blanket, and he hasn’t got any further than that.

It hasn’t lit since 5:52, when she wrote *are you watching this* from a couch on Del Playa and he wrote back from the Fishbowl. That’s six hours of somebody’s television. At five past twelve it lights.

Six hours of it. She hung up on her mother and then she wrote to him to ask what his people do.
He lies on his back in the dark and answers with his thumb.

s07b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:40 AM · THE BRICK, THIRD FLOOR
body: In the lobby of the Pacifica Library the newspaper rack has today’s *Los Angeles Times*, and above the fold the National Palace in Port-au-Prince has come down: the long white building with the dome, the dome dropped onto the floors beneath it and the wings bowed in. The stack hasn’t been touched. On the television over the circulation desk CNN runs with the sound off, a street of gray dust and people standing in it, and the girl at the desk keeps her eyes on her scanner when he goes by.

Up on three the carrels are full and quiet in a way that isn’t only the library’s. She has a double one at the end by the window, the kind somebody knocked the partition out of, and she’s in his flannel with a textbook open that he has never seen her carry. *Oceanography 1*. Undeclared, she told him in December, and meant it; she signed up for this one, she says now, because she surfs, and she wanted to know what was hitting her.
“I read the chapter at three in the morning,” she says. “Sol and Tomás and me on the floor in front of CNN till four. I had to know what it was.” She turns the book around to him. “So. Look.”
It’s a map of the Caribbean with the sea floor colored in, and lines across it with small arrows on them. She puts her finger on one.

“This is the Caribbean plate. This up here is North America. They’re not crashing into each other — it’s not that kind. They’re sliding past. Sideways.” She puts her two hands together on the carrel, edge to edge, and slides one forward along the other. “Except they don’t slide. They stick. For a hundred years, two hundred, they stick, and all that time it’s loading up, and then one afternoon it lets go at once. Strike-slip. There’s a fault that runs right along under the city.” She takes her hands back. “No warning. It says that in bold. There isn’t any warning, ever, for this kind.”
“Will it do it again?”

“It already did. Aftershocks. For weeks, it says.” She opens the book again to a diagram, a long line with bright spots along it. “And the push doesn’t go away. It moves down the fault to the next place that’s stuck.” She taps the city on the map. “They built the capital right on top of it. Everybody does. San Francisco. LA. You build where the harbor is, and the harbor is where the ground came apart a long time ago.”
She closes the book on her pencil.
“I’ve never understood anything in a textbook before,” Skye says. “I wish I didn’t understand this one.”

He has his own homework: the first half of *Frankenstein* for Hale by Thursday, one of eleven novels in fourteen weeks. She takes it out of his hands before he has it open, a used paperback with the creature on the cover, and turns to the title page, and reads it to him, every word where it was put, her voice gone down low for it:
*Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould me Man, did I solicit thee / From darkness to promote me?*
She hands it back.
“That’s the line,” she says. “That’s the whole show.”
And she goes back to the plates.

For half an hour they work. She slips her shoes off under the carrel and puts her feet in his lap, and does her reading with a yellow highlighter she keeps capping and uncapping, and he reads Captain Walton writing home to his sister from the ice. At twenty past ten the highlighter stops. Her head comes down on his shoulder, heavy, and her breathing goes long and slow over the Caribbean.

He doesn’t move. He reads forty pages with one hand, turning them with his thumb against the edge of the carrel — Walton and the stranger on the ice, then Geneva, a mother, a boy who wants to know how everything works — with her hair against his jaw and her feet warm on his leg, and she smells of the beach and of his own shirt. A girl at the next carrel recognizes her; he watches it happen, the double take and the quick glance at him, and the girl goes back to her own book.
At ten to eleven Skye wakes up on him with the seam of his sleeve printed on her cheek.

choices.text: “You snore in Swedish.”
response: “You snore in Swedish.”
“The *Saab* is Swedish. I’m from Burbank.”
“The Saab’s GM.”
“Don’t.” She puts her hand over his mouth, and keeps it there while she finds her shoes with her feet.

Her eleven o’clock is across campus. She goes at five to, at a run, in his flannel, and leaves *Oceanography 1* on his half of the carrel — by mistake, or not. He puts it in his bag on top of Mary Shelley and takes it with him.

choices.text: “Go back to sleep. I’ve got a hundred pages.”
response: “Go back to sleep. I’ve got a hundred pages.”
She does, for ten more minutes, on purpose; he can tell it’s on purpose because she arranges herself first, his arm moved to where she wants it and her cheek on the other side of the seam.

Her eleven o’clock is across campus. She goes at five to, at a run, in his flannel, and leaves *Oceanography 1* on his half of the carrel — by mistake, or not. He puts it in his bag on top of Mary Shelley and takes it with him.

choices.text: “Explain the plates again. I like hearing you know things.”
response: “Explain the plates again. I like hearing you know things.”

She sits up and looks at him for a moment with her hair flat on one side, and does it again, and this time she uses his hands for the plates — his left for North America, his right for the Caribbean — and slides them past each other on the carrel, slowly, and holds them still at the place where they catch.
“There,” she says. “That’s a hundred years.”

Her eleven o’clock is across campus. She goes at five to, at a run, in his flannel, and leaves *Oceanography 1* on his half of the carrel — by mistake, or not. He puts it in his bag on top of Mary Shelley and takes it with him.

s13.slug: WEDNESDAY · 5:10 PM · THE SAAB, THE BLUFF ROAD
body: The sun has gone into the water by ten past five, but the sky is still lit from underneath: orange along the bottom and then a long clean blue going dark at the top, and the Saab is parked on the bluff road with its top down and its nose at all of it.

Her phone goes off on the dash. She looks at the name and lets it ring. She takes his hand off his knee and puts it on the gearshift and puts hers over it, and leaves them there through three more rings, and then she answers on speaker.
“I’m looking at you in an apron,” Corinne says.
“It’s Becca’s.”

“I don’t know who Becca is. There are eleven pictures of you on a *Sweetwater* fan forum and four on TwitPic, and the forum ones have a caption — *Cassidy says your name* — with three exclamation points. That’s in two hours. It’s adorable.” A keystroke in Beverly Hills. “It is also not managed. I have a statement. ‘Skye is heartbroken by the devastation in Haiti and was proud to —’”
Skye says the next part along with her, silently, with her eyes shut, and gets every word.
“— and there’s a boy at the back of every one of them,” Corinne says.
“He was holding the cash box.”

body.text: “Your boyfriend’s wall is a public utility. He *commented*. ‘Hi, Glenwood Ave.’”
“Your boyfriend’s wall is a public utility. He deleted one, and a man named Tommy put it back with *lol*.”
“Your boyfriend’s wall is a public utility. His friend count went up by twenty-three in an afternoon. Who *are* these people?”
“Your boyfriend’s wall is a public utility. Forty-seven comments under a video of my client, and he hasn’t touched it. Tell him I said good.”

body: Jack looks at the phone. Skye looks at Jack, and for the first time since it rang, her mouth goes up at one corner.
“The network called me at three,” Corinne says. “They wanted to know who the boy is. I said a friend from school.”
“He’s not a friend from school.” Skye picks a fleck of bark off the dash and flicks it over the side. “He’s a boyfriend from school. It’s in the system, Corinne. I put it there.”
“I’m aware of where it is.” Another keystroke. “And thank you for taking down the car.”
“Not for you.”
A click on the line, and another voice, warmer and farther off: Debbie, on the extension in Studio City. “Baby, people want to see you care.”

“I cared for three hours in an apron, Mother.” Skye opens her eyes. “It’s twenty-dollar bills, Corinne. You can’t release twenty-dollar bills.” And then, as level as the last of the light on the water: “The girl at the table said no pictures. She was right.”
There is a silence in Beverly Hills long enough to hear the surf come up the bluff.
“We’ll talk tomorrow,” Corinne says.
“We will,” Skye says, and hangs up, and doesn’t move her hand. His is still under it on the gearshift. He turns it over, so her fingers lie in his palm.

Below the bluff the tide is going out over the reef, white where it breaks and then dark, and a pelican goes along the line of it low enough to touch. They stay till the color is gone and the platforms come on out on the black water, one and then another. She asks him what the creature wants yet, and he says he’s only on page forty, and she says the creature wants what everybody wants and she isn’t going to tell him what that is until he’s done. At eight she drives them to Lupe’s truck, and they eat carne asada out of foil in the car with the dome light on, and she gets salsa on the cuff of his flannel and says it’s hers now anyway.
After, she balls up the foil and drops it in the bag at her feet, and puts the key in, and doesn’t turn it.
“Your world or mine?”

choices.text: *St. Brendan’s. It’s open late tonight.*
choices.key: Wednesday night you took Skye into St. Brendan’s, open late for Haiti.
response: “Mine’s open till midnight,” he says. “Father said so at the twelve-ten.”
She turns the key.

choices.text: *Your porch.*
choices.key: Wednesday night you went back to Skye’s porch on Del Playa.
response: “Yours,” he says. “The porch.”
She turns the key.

s13a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:20 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR (OPEN LATE)

body.title: A sign taped to the church door
body.text: OPEN UNTIL MIDNIGHT FOR HAITI. COME IN. —Fr. G.

body: St. Brendan’s has its doors propped and most of its lights off. Confessions were over at a quarter to nine; the box at the back is dark. Up the nave the hull of the ceiling goes away into shadow over the pews, and the blue glass is black, and the only real light is at the Marian shrine on the right, where the votive rack is nearly full — three tiers of small flames in red glass — and the light from it moves on the wall. Four people are praying, scattered, one to a pew. At the far end, by the sacristy door, Father Osei is turning off a light. He sees them, and goes through the door, and leaves them be.
Skye stops just inside with her hand on the back of the last pew. She has never been inside a Catholic church at night, and she tells him so in a whisper.
“I’ve shot in three,” she whispers. “Day for night. There was craft services in the confessional.”

He takes her up the side aisle to the rack. She wants to light one; she has never lit one. He shows her: the long taper out of the sand tray, a flame borrowed from somebody else’s candle, the wick, the taper back in the sand. The slot wants money. She has a twenty and nothing smaller; he has four quarters he was saving for the dryer, and two of them go in, and she listens to each one land.
She lights it with both hands on the taper and doesn’t breathe until it takes.
Under the shrine, in the moving light, there is the brass plate. She bends to read it.

body.title: A brass plate under the shrine
body.text: NORA GRACE CALLOWAY · 1989–2009 · “LORD, TO WHOM SHALL WE GO?”

body: “Who was she?”

He tells her what everybody knows. A sophomore; a soprano; she sang in this choir. She went out to the Point one night last April and fell from the wall. It was in the paper. Newman put the plate up in the fall.
Skye looks at it a while, and draws the taper out of the sand again. “For her too,” she says, “since I’m here,” and lights a second one beside the first, and he feeds the slot the last two quarters.
They stand there. Somebody at the back opens the door to leave and the night comes up the aisle, and every flame in the rack leans and comes back.
Up by the altar, in the dark, one lamp is burning that isn’t at the shrine: a small red glass on a chain beside the tabernacle. She has seen it. She points with her chin.
“Why is that one red? It’s the only one up there.”
“It means He’s there.”
“Who?”
“Him. In the tabernacle. The bread from Mass.” He doesn’t lower his voice any further than it already is. “It stays lit as long as He’s in there. It’s somebody’s job to make sure it never goes out.”
She looks at the little red lamp a long time, with her arms folded inside his flannel. “You think that’s really Him. In a box. In a building in Santa Barbara, with the lights off.”
“Yes.”
“Huh,” Skye says, very softly, and turns back to her candles.
“Say one for them,” Skye says. “From me. I don’t know the words.”

response: He kneels on the step of the shrine, and she kneels next to him because he did. He says it slowly, a phrase at a time, and she comes along half a word behind him to the end — *Holy Mary, Mother of God* — with the candlelight on her face. At the end she says *Amen* late, by herself, into the quiet, and laughs at herself without making a sound.

response: He gives her the first line. She says it back once, perfectly, every syllable where he put it, a line she’ll be tested on. Then she says it again, lower, to the two candles.
“That one was for real,” she whispers.
He couldn’t tell the difference. She says, when he tells her, that she couldn’t either.

response: “I pray for whoever’s under there to know somebody’s coming.”
She looks at the two candles she lit. “That’s what I’d want.”
“That’s what you said.”
She takes his hand down at their sides, where the four people in the pews can’t see it, and holds it there, low, while the four people in the pews go on praying.

s13c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:05 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD → THE SAAB
body: Out in the courtyard the olive tree has the streetlight caught up in it, and the sprinkler stands in the dead grass with its head cocked, as it has all year. She sits on the edge of the planter under the tree and pulls him down next to her by his sleeve.
“Tell me who everybody was,” she says. “At the table.”
So he tells her. Becca, from Idaho, who lent her the apron.
“I know. She told me. I want to adopt her.”
Clare, with the violin, a sophomore at Newman. The guy who brought two flats of water you can’t send anywhere, and stayed to hold the case.
“Kevin. From the glass room. He held it like it had a baby in it.”
Ted, and Ted’s onion.
“I could smell it from the box.”
The redhead in the sunglasses.
“Laney. She introduced herself.” Skye stretches her legs out on the flagstones. “She hates me. I’m going to get her a present.”
And the guy with the flyers.
“Songs for Haiti,” Skye says. “I took one.”
He gets to the end of the table and stops there. Skye doesn’t ask. She reaches up and turns his medal right side out where it had flipped on its chain, and leaves her fingers on it a little.
At the Saab, under the streetlight on Ocean Road, she leans back against her door with her hands in the front pocket of his flannel, and takes them out.
“I want to take you home,” she says. “I want that a lot. And I’m too sad tonight to be any good at it.”
She looks at him under the light.
“Saturday.”
The streetlight buzzes over them. Somewhere down Ocean Road a car alarm starts and gives up. “It’s in my calendar,” she says. “In pen.”

body.text: “And I wrote your brother. In capitals.” She pokes him in the chest. “I need the address.”
Her finger finds the shape of the RAZR through his Carhartt pocket and taps it. “And you still owe me a face.”

She drives him back to Delgado and stops at the curb with the engine running, and he gets out. Up on four the lounge light is on, and the lobby is lit behind its glass doors, and he stands on the curb and looks up at it.

response: He takes out the RAZR and opens the one he has carried around shut since Thursday, and she doesn’t look at the screen. She looks at him, under the streetlight, for as long as it takes. It’s the window, and the surf through her. When he looks up she has seen whatever she wanted to see; it’s there in her mouth. “Saturday,” she says, and kisses him.

She drives him back to Delgado and stops at the curb with the engine running, and he gets out. Up on four the lounge light is on, and the lobby is lit behind its glass doors, and he stands on the curb and looks up at it.

s13b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:20 PM · DEL PLAYA, THE PORCH
body: The porch at Sol’s house leans toward the sea; it always has. The swing hangs off it on two chains with every blanket off her bed piled on it, and his Carhartt on top. Tomás’s boards stand against the rail. The heater inside is still broken, and it’s warmer out here than in. Through the front window Sol’s television is on CNN with the sound off, Haiti going all night in a lit square behind their heads, and from somewhere deeper in the house, on Sol’s record player, a woman is singing low over a drum machine and something like strings.

Her room is through the door and down the hall. They don’t go in. She sits down on the swing and he sits down beside her, and she pulls the blankets up over both of them, and the swing moves under them and settles.

She doesn’t sleep. She sits with her knees up under the blankets and her chin on them, and watches the screen through the glass over his shoulder. Without any sound, men in a street of gray dust are pulling at a slab of concrete with their hands. The picture changes to a man on a phone, and back to the slab.

Sol made a pot of rice last night at nine, she tells him, because Sol’s mother makes rice when something terrible happens, and none of them ate it, and at two in the morning all three of them ate it standing up out of the pot. “It was very bad rice,” Skye says. “I had seconds. Don’t tell Sol either part.”
After a while her legs come across his lap under the blankets, and her feet find the warm place against his hip and settle there. She’s in his flannel still, with the salsa on the cuff.
“The prayer from the car,” she says. “The Mary one. Who is she, exactly? I know who she is. I mean what is she, to you. You pray to his mother.”
“With her. You ask her to pray with you.”
“So she’s your agent.”
“Agents take ten percent.”
“What does she take?”
“Nothing. She just asks.” He thinks about how to say the rest. “She’s the one who stood there. At the end. When everybody else ran.”
Skye watches the slab through the window. “She stood there,” she says. “I can see why you’d want her in the room.”
Inside the house the record turns over to something slower.
“What do you pray,” she says. “For people under a building.”

response: He says it slowly, a phrase at a time, and she follows half a word behind him with the television’s light moving on her face — *pray for us sinners* — and her lips working at it. At the end she says *Amen* late, by herself, to the porch, and laughs at herself without a sound.

response: He gives her the first line. She says it back once, perfectly, and then again, quieter, with her eyes on the men and the slab through the window.
“Did the second one count more?”
“They both count.”
“Good,” she says. “I couldn’t tell the difference either.”

She watches the slab on the screen. “That’s what I’d want.”
“That’s what you said.”
Under the blankets she finds his hand and lays it on her knee and keeps hers on top of it.

body.title: A card propped against Theo’s lamp
body.text:
SIGMA RHO
requests the honor of
Theodore Ashby Vance

body: “Congratulations,” Jack says from his bed.

“They want me,” Theo says. “It’s very flattering. They also want me to shave a lacrosse stick.” He sits on the end of his bed to unlace his shoes. “Brooks would like it known that he paid for two pictures this afternoon. He would like it known in writing. I’ve told him the Church doesn’t issue receipts for vanity, and he’s taking it to the chapter.”
“What’s a chapter?”

“Eleven men in a basement deciding what I’m worth. I came in third, behind a boy from Encino and a keg.” He takes off the Rolex and lays it face-up on the nightstand, and turns the lamp off, and the card goes dark with it.

body: Across the room Theo’s breathing has already gone slow; he could always do that, go under like a stone into a pond. Jack lies with the phone open over his face and the cursor going, and the building ticks around him after midnight, pipes and somebody’s door and the elevator going down empty. He has a thank-you to pass along.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’
